Lower Back Pain After Sitting All Day? What Office Workers in Thane Should Know

Dr. Surabhi Vaidya · BAMS (Ayurveda) Charak Health Solutions · Raymond TenX Habitat, Thane West
📅 November 2026 ⏱ 6 min read 🏷 Spine & Posture

You leave home for work, sit through a long commute, spend several hours at your desk, and return home with an aching lower back.

Perhaps standing up after sitting feels uncomfortable. Sometimes the stiffness improves after walking. On other days, the pain continues into the evening.

For people working in Thane, Mumbai and surrounding business districts, long hours of sitting and commuting are a familiar part of daily life.

But there is an important distinction to understand:

Lower back pain after sitting does not automatically mean you have a slipped disc or permanent spinal damage.

Several factors may contribute to back discomfort, and identifying them can help you take appropriate action.

Why does your lower back hurt after sitting?

Lower back pain is common and can arise from muscles, joints, discs, nerves and other structures.

In many cases, a single precise cause cannot be identified.

1. Staying in one position for too long

Remaining seated for extended periods may make an already sensitive lower back uncomfortable.

The problem is not necessarily that one sitting posture is dangerous. Rather, people often feel better when they can change positions and move comfortably throughout the day.

2. Reduced physical activity

If much of your day involves sitting, you may have fewer opportunities to walk, stretch or maintain physical strength.

Appropriate movement and regular exercise can play an important role in managing many types of lower back pain.

3. Reduced muscle endurance

Muscles supporting your spine and trunk help you perform daily activities.

Limited strength or endurance can contribute to difficulty tolerating certain activities, although this is only one possible factor.

4. Disc-related or nerve-related conditions

Sometimes lower back pain is associated with an irritated spinal nerve or a disc problem.

Pain extending into the buttock or leg, especially with tingling, numbness or weakness, may require a closer examination.

However, back pain alone does not establish that a person has a disc injury.

Five practical habits for a more comfortable working day

  1. Change positions regularly: Avoid feeling that you must maintain one perfect posture for the entire day. Sit, stand and move when possible, especially if remaining in the same position increases discomfort.
  2. Include short movement breaks: You can take brief walking breaks between meetings, during calls or after longer periods at your desk. There is no single compulsory schedule that suits everyone. Find a pattern you can follow consistently.
  3. Adjust your workstation: Position your chair, screen and keyboard so that working feels comfortable. Keep commonly used items within easy reach and allow yourself enough space to change positions.
  4. Continue suitable physical activity: Walking and appropriately selected exercise are commonly recommended for uncomplicated lower back pain. Build activity gradually, according to your symptoms and physical abilities.
  5. Do not ignore recurring symptoms: An occasional episode of back discomfort may improve with time. However, repeated pain that disrupts work, travel or sleep deserves attention, particularly when symptoms are changing.

Does lower back pain always require an MRI?

No.

Routine imaging is generally not recommended for uncomplicated lower back pain without concerning clinical findings.

An MRI or other investigation may be appropriate when a clinician suspects a serious condition, identifies significant neurological changes, or believes imaging would influence management.

Imaging findings must also be interpreted alongside symptoms and clinical examination.

When should you consult a doctor?

Arrange a medical assessment if your pain persists, repeatedly returns, interferes with everyday activities, or begins travelling down a leg.

⚠️ Urgent Medical Warning Signs

Seek urgent medical assessment if you experience:

  • New difficulty controlling your bladder or bowels
  • Numbness around the groin, genitals, or saddle area
  • Severe or worsening weakness in your legs (difficulty lifting your foot or standing)
  • Significant trauma or fall followed by sudden severe back pain
  • Back pain accompanied by fever, chills, or unexplained weight loss
Some of these symptoms may indicate Cauda Equina Syndrome or acute spinal cord compression requiring immediate emergency hospital care.
